lesson.title: One Kind of Atom: Understanding Elements and the Periodic Table
lesson.summary: This section defines elements as pure substances of one atomic number and shows how the periodic table organizes them by shared chemical behavior.
lesson.body:
An atom, as the previous section explained, is defined by its number of protons, its atomic number. An element is a pure substance made up entirely of atoms that all share that same atomic number. Gold is an element because every atom in a pure gold bar has exactly 79 protons; oxygen is an element because every oxygen atom has exactly 8 protons. Because an element cannot be broken down into a simpler substance by ordinary chemical means, only nuclear reactions, which are far more extreme than chemical reactions, can change the number of protons in a nucleus, elements serve as the basic chemical building blocks from which everything else in this course is constructed. Chemists currently recognize 118 confirmed elements, each identified by a one or two letter symbol drawn largely from Latin or Greek names: H for hydrogen, O for oxygen, Fe for iron, from the Latin ferrum, and Au for gold, from the Latin aurum.

These 118 elements are organized into the periodic table, one of the most information dense charts in all of science. Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, left to right and top to bottom, but the table's real power comes from its columns, called groups, and rows, called periods. Elements in the same group share similar chemical behavior because, as you will see in later sections on atomic structure, they have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell. Sodium and potassium, both in group 1, react vigorously with water in strikingly similar ways, while helium, neon, and argon, in group 18, are so unreactive that they are called the noble gases. This grouping is not decoration; it lets a chemist predict how an unfamiliar element will behave just from its position on the table.

The periodic table also splits elements into three broad categories: metals, nonmetals, and metalloids. Metals, which occupy the majority of the table, are generally shiny, malleable, and good conductors of heat and electricity; iron, copper, and aluminum are everyday examples. Nonmetals, clustered in the upper right, tend to be poor conductors and include gases like nitrogen and oxygen as well as solids like sulfur and carbon. Metalloids, such as silicon and germanium, sit along the zigzag line dividing metals from nonmetals and show intermediate properties, which is exactly why silicon is the workhorse material of the semiconductor industry: it conducts electricity, but only under the right conditions.

It is worth being precise about the difference between an atom and an element, since the two words are often used loosely and interchangeably in casual speech. An atom is a single particle. An element is the category of substance defined by a shared atomic number, and also the name for a pure sample made of nothing but that one kind of atom. When chemists say iron is an element, they mean both that iron atoms all share atomic number 26 and that a block of pure iron metal contains nothing but those atoms. In the next section, you will see what happens when different elements combine: atoms of different elements bonding together to form compounds, whose properties can be wildly different from the elements that make them up.
